summary: For ages 7–9, teach animal communication as a goal-directed system (sender → signal → receiver → response) across at least four channels — sound, movement/dance, light, scent/chemical, and body language — each paired with a clear purpose: attracting mates, warning of danger, locating food, or defending territory. The central idea is that a signal only matters when another animal receives it and changes what it does, and that animals carry real information through many senses, not human-style words.
misconceptions: 'Animals only communicate with sounds' — many use scent, light, movement/dance, and body posture.
'Animals talk in words / have language like ours' — they exchange specific signals, not human-style sentences.
'Communication is always to be friendly' — many signals warn, threaten, or claim territory.
'A signal works on its own' — it only matters if another animal receives and responds to it.
'Bright colours/lights and dances are just for show' — they carry real messages (mate quality, food direction, warning).

activities.title: Send the signal: operate a communication loop
steps: Take the role of the sender: pick an animal, choose a channel (sound, dance, light, scent, or body language), and choose a message (danger, mate, food, or territory).
Transmit the signal and watch whether the receiver reads it and acts — flee an alarm call, approach a display, follow a scent trail.
Enter a honeybee waggle-dance mode: set the dance's angle (direction) and duration (distance), then watch hive-mates fly off to the correct flower — or the wrong one when the dance is off.

Try sending a channel that does not suit the setting (a light flash in bright daylight that is washed out, or a visual body-posture display in dark, murky deep water where the receiver cannot see it) and observe the receiver fail to get the message.
activities.insight: A signal is not just a sound or a show — it is information that only works when a receiver reads it and changes its behaviour, and the channel must suit the environment and what the receiver can sense.

activities.title: Signal-channel gallery
steps: Explore a scene of animals and reveal each one's channel: hear a sound clip (whale song, birdsong, wolf howl, alarm call), watch a movement/dance (honeybee waggle, peacock display), see a light glow (firefly flash, deep-sea bioluminescence), see a scent puff (ant trail, dog scent-marking, moth pheromone), or read a body-language posture (dog posture, cat tail, gorilla chest-beat).
For each animal revealed, read its purpose card: mate, danger, food, or territory.
Collect at least one example from each of the five channels so the survey covers the full sensory range, not just sound.
activities.insight: Animals 'talk' through scent, light, movement, and body posture as well as sound — communication spans many senses.

activities.title: Hands-on ant-trail investigation
steps: If a live ant trail to a food source is available, first predict what will happen if part of the path is wiped away.
Wipe a section of the trail with a wet cloth and watch what the ants do.
Describe what the wiping tells you about how the ants were finding their way.
activities.insight: If the ants lose their way where the trail was wiped, that suggests they were following a scent message left on the path, not simply 'knowing' the way. Wiping removes the scent, so the message is gone. (Some ants also use sight or landmarks, so the effect can vary.)

activities.title: Match signals to purposes and channels
steps: Match each signal to its purpose (e.g. alarm call → warn of danger; waggle dance → show food direction; scent trail → lead to food; display → attract a mate).
Sort animal examples by channel (sound, dance, light, scent, body language).
Answer a short question about why a signal needs both a sender and a receiver, giving a non-sound example.
Respond to the prompt: 'Only animals that make sounds can communicate — a silent animal can't send any message. Is that right?' Name a silent channel and say what it tells the receiver.
activities.insight: Communication is any signal carrying information to a receiver; naming a working non-sound example shows you understand it is not limited to noise or words.

activities.title: Optional hook: ask a zoologist
steps: Pose questions to an in-role animal behaviourist about how they decode a signal, such as how researchers worked out what whale song or the waggle dance means.

Follow up with the probe questions: who a firefly's flash is for and what it says; why a bird sings and what job the song does; how nest-mates learn where food is when many ants rely mainly on scent rather than sight or sound; and whether a growling dog is communicating.
activities.insight: Decoding real animal signals is detective work about information, mates, danger, food and territory — curiosity about the topic is grounded in how messages are read.

checkQuestion: Your friend says: 'Only animals that make sounds can communicate — a silent animal can't send any message.' Is your friend right? How might a firefly or an ant that makes no sound still send a message to another animal?
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong. Communicating means sending a message another animal can read, and it doesn't have to be sound. A firefly flashes patterns of light to attract a mate; ants leave a scent trail so others can follow it to food; bees dance to show the direction and distance of flowers; and many animals use body language, like a dog raising its hackles. Sound is only one channel — light, scent, movement and posture all carry messages too.
